claim: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global health crisis, with bacterial AMR implicated in approximately 4.95 million deaths in 2019.
source: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global health crisis, with bacterial AMR implicated in approximately 4.95 million deaths in 2019 and predictions estimating up to 10 million deaths per year by 2050 (Murray et al., 2022; O'Neill, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Murray et al., 2022 and O'Neill, 2016.

claim: Bacterial AMR is predicted to cause up to 10 million deaths per year by 2050.
source: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global health crisis, with bacterial AMR implicated in approximately 4.95 million deaths in 2019 and predictions estimating up to 10 million deaths per year by 2050 (Murray et al., 2022; O'Neill, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Murray et al., 2022 and O'Neill, 2016.

claim: Bacterial cell walls are mainly composed of peptidoglycan (PG) and are crucial for survival.
source: Bacterial cell walls, mainly composed of peptidoglycan (PG) and crucial for survival, serve as a primary target for antimicrobials.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell wall composition.

claim: Bacterial cell walls serve as a primary target for antimicrobials.
source: Bacterial cell walls, mainly composed of peptidoglycan (PG) and crucial for survival, serve as a primary target for antimicrobials.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in antimicrobial research.

claim: The discovery of conventional PG-inhibiting small molecules is impeded by fewer choices and increasing resistance.
source: However, the discovery of conventional PG-inhibiting small molecules is impeded by fewer choices and increasing resistance (Bonomo, 2017; Drawz and Bonomo, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonomo, 2017 and Drawz and Bonomo, 2010.

claim: Naturally occurring PG-lysing enzymes secreted by bacteria for competition in polymicrobial environments remain underexplored for AMR treatment.
source: The naturally occurring PG-lysing enzymes, secreted by bacteria for competition in polymicrobial environments (Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Whitney et al., 2017), remain underexplored for AMR treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Whitney et al., 2017.

claim: The type VI secretion system (T6SS) can directly inject PG-lysing enzymes and other antibacterial toxins into neighboring microbes.
source: As a widespread molecular weapon in Gram-negative bacteria, the type VI secretion system (T6SS) can directly inject PG-lysing enzymes and other antibacterial toxins into neighboring microbes and anti-eukaryotic toxins to yeast and mammalian cells (Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Le et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2009; Mougous et al., 2006; Pei et al., 2022; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Trunk et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Le et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2009; Mougous et al., 2006; Pei et al., 2022; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Trunk et al., 2018.

claim: The T6SS can inject anti-eukaryotic toxins to yeast and mammalian cells.
source: As a widespread molecular weapon in Gram-negative bacteria, the type VI secretion system (T6SS) can directly inject PG-lysing enzymes and other antibacterial toxins into neighboring microbes and anti-eukaryotic toxins to yeast and mammalian cells (Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Le et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2009; Mougous et al., 2006; Pei et al., 2022; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Trunk et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Le et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2009; Mougous et al., 2006; Pei et al., 2022; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Trunk et al., 2018.

claim: The conserved structure of T6SS consists of a double tubular structure, a baseplate TssEFGK complex, and a transmembrane TssJLM complex.
source: The conserved structure of T6SS consists of a double tubular structure, a baseplate TssEFGK complex, and a transmembrane TssJLM complex (Basler et al., 2012; Brunet et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Basler et al., 2012; Brunet et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019.

claim: The T6SS inner tube is made of stacks of Hcp hexamers.
source: A spear-like inner tube, made of stacks of Hcp hexamers, is ejected outward upon contraction of an outer sheath made of stacks of TssB/C hexamers, and a VgrG-PAAR spike complex sitting atop the Hcp tube is delivered concomitantly (Mougous et al., 2006; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Shneider et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mougous et al., 2006; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Shneider et al., 2013.

claim: The T6SS outer sheath is made of stacks of TssB/C hexamers.
source: A spear-like inner tube, made of stacks of Hcp hexamers, is ejected outward upon contraction of an outer sheath made of stacks of TssB/C hexamers, and a VgrG-PAAR spike complex sitting atop the Hcp tube is delivered concomitantly (Mougous et al., 2006; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Shneider et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mougous et al., 2006; Pukatzki et al., 2006; Shneider et al., 2013.

claim: T6SS-elicited damages are largely dependent on the secreted effectors rather than the penetration.
source: Although the ejected Hcp spear can penetrate neighboring bacterial cells, T6SS-elicited damages are largely dependent on the secreted effectors rather than the penetration (Kamal et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2019; Vettiger and Basler, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kamal et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2019; Vettiger and Basler, 2016.

claim: Known T6SS effectors display diverse functions including damaging the cell wall and membrane, DNase, metal scavenging, and targeting host cell actin cytoskeleton.
source: Numerous T6SS effectors have been predicted in Gram-negative bacteria, and known effectors display diverse functions including damaging the cell wall and membrane, DNase, metal scavenging, and targeting host cell actin cytoskeleton (Dong et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2015; Pukatzki et al., 2007; Russell et al., 2012; Salomon et al., 2014; Si et al., 2017; Whitney et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Dong et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2015; Pukatzki et al., 2007; Russell et al., 2012; Salomon et al., 2014; Si et al., 2017; Whitney et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024.

claim: PG-targeting effectors are most commonly associated with the T6SSs.
source: Despite the functional diversity of T6SS effectors, PG-targeting effectors seem to be most commonly associated with the T6SSs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of effector diversity.

claim: The conserved structure of PG comprises repeating disaccharide units of N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), with a short peptide attached to each NAM.
source: The conserved structure of PG comprises repeating disaccharide units of N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), with a short peptide (most commonly L-Ala-D-Glu-m-DAP-D-Ala-D-Ala) attached to each NAM (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vollmer et al., 2008.

claim: Adjacent peptide chains of PG are cross-linked, forming a continuous network that envelops bacterial cells.
source: Adjacent peptide chains of PG are cross-linked, forming a continuous network that envelops bacterial cells (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vollmer et al., 2008.

claim: T6SS effectors known to target PG fall into two categories: T6SS amidase/endopeptidase (Tae) families cleaving the peptides and T6SS glycoside hydrolase (Tge) families cleaving the glycan backbone.
source: T6SS effectors known to target PG fall into two categories, T6SS amidase/endopeptidase (Tae) families cleaving the peptides and T6SS glycoside hydrolase (Tge) families cleaving the glycan backbone.
evidence: This is a classification based on established knowledge of T6SS effectors.

claim: Tae effectors have been found to cleave bonds between D-Glu and mDAP, between mDAP and D-Ala, and between NAM and L-Ala.
source: Tae effectors have been found to cleave bonds between D-Glu and mDAP, between mDAP and D-Ala, and between NAM and L-Ala (Russell et al., 2011; Russell et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2018; Hernandez et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Russell et al., 2011; Russell et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2018; Hernandez et al., 2020.

claim: Tge effectors possess β-(1-4)-N-acetyl-muramidase activities and N-acetylglucosaminidase activities.
source: Tge effectors possess β-(1-4)-N-acetyl-muramidase activities and N-acetylglucosaminidase activities (Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2012; Whitney et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2012; Whitney et al., 2013.

claim: Tse4 in Acinetobacter baumannii cleaves both the glycan strand and the cross-linked peptide cross-bridge.
source: The recent discovery of Tse4 in Acinetobacter baumannii, cleaving both the glycan strand and the cross-linked peptide cross-bridge, suggests that dual enzymatic activities could be found in a single effector (Le et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Le et al., 2021.

claim: Dual enzymatic activities in a single T6SS effector are rare.
source: However, such bifunctionality among effectors is rare.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited examples of bifunctional effectors.

claim: Aeromonas dhakensis is a ubiquitous waterborne pathogen that can cause soft tissue infection and bacteremia in fish and humans.
source: As a ubiquitous waterborne pathogen, Aeromonas dhakensis can cause soft tissue infection and bacteremia in fish and humans (Chen et al., 2016; Kitagawa et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016; Kitagawa et al., 2020.

claim: The T6SS of A. dhakensis type strain SSU is active under laboratory conditions.
source: The T6SS of A. dhakensis type strain SSU is active under laboratory conditions and can secrete three known antimicrobial effectors, a membrane-targeting TseC, a lysozyme-like TseP, and a nuclease TseI (Liang et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2021b; Pei et al., 2020; Suarez et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2021b; Pei et al., 2020; Suarez et al., 2008.

claim: The T6SS of A. dhakensis SSU can secrete three known antimicrobial effectors: TseC, TseP, and TseI.
source: The T6SS of A. dhakensis type strain SSU is active under laboratory conditions and can secrete three known antimicrobial effectors, a membrane-targeting TseC, a lysozyme-like TseP, and a nuclease TseI (Liang et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2021b; Pei et al., 2020; Suarez et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2021b; Pei et al., 2020; Suarez et al., 2008.

claim: TseP expression can restore the T6SS secretion in the Δ3eff mutant lacking all three effector genes.
source: Our previous findings have established that TseP serves a structural role because its expression can restore the T6SS secretion in the Δ3eff mutant lacking all three effector genes, and the C-terminal domain, TsePC, possesses lysozyme activities (Liang et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2021b.

claim: The C-terminal domain of TseP (TsePC) possesses lysozyme activities.
source: Our previous findings have established that TseP serves a structural role because its expression can restore the T6SS secretion in the Δ3eff mutant lacking all three effector genes, and the C-terminal domain, TsePC, possesses lysozyme activities (Liang et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2021b.

claim: TsePN is capable of cleaving the peptide link between NAM and L-Ala as an amidase.
source: This study unveils that TsePN is capable of cleaving the peptide link between NAM and L-Ala as an amidase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TsePN exhibits approximately 10% higher GC content than TsePC.
source: Additionally, TsePN exhibits approximately 10% higher GC content than TsePC, and homologs of TsePN and TsePC exist independently in divergent species.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Homologs of TsePN and TsePC exist independently in divergent species.
source: Additionally, TsePN exhibits approximately 10% higher GC content than TsePC, and homologs of TsePN and TsePC exist independently in divergent species.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The disparity in GC content and the presence of domain-specific homologs suggest an evolutionary fusion event.
source: This disparity in GC content and the presence of domain-specific homologs suggest an evolutionary fusion event.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GC content analysis and homolog distribution.

claim: TsePC can be engineered to hydrolyze resistant Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis cells.
source: We further show that TsePC can be engineered to hydrolyze resistant Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis cells, conferring the T6SS with the capability to kill Gram-positive bacteria in a contact-independent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Engineered TsePC confers the T6SS with the capability to kill Gram-positive bacteria in a contact-independent manner.
source: We further show that TsePC can be engineered to hydrolyze resistant Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis cells, conferring the T6SS with the capability to kill Gram-positive bacteria in a contact-independent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The Δ3eff mutant failed to secrete Hcp.
source: Consistent with our previous results (Liang et al., 2021b), protein secretion assays show that the Δ3eff mutant, akin to the T6SS null ΔvasK, failed to secrete Hcp (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and by citation to Liang et al., 2021b.

claim: Complementation with TseP and TsePN, but not TsePC, restored Hcp secretion in the Δ3eff mutant.
source: Complementation with TseP and TsePN, but not TsePC, restored Hcp secretion, despite at a reduced level relative to the wild-type (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Complementation with both TseP and TsePN, but not TsePC, restored sheath assembly in the Δ3eff mutant.
source: Fluorescence microscopy analysis showed that complementation with both TseP and TsePN, but not the TsePC, restored sheath assembly (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: TsePN was secreted in the Δ3eff mutant, but TsePC was not.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that TsePN, but not TsePC, was secreted (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TsePC was secreted in both wild-type and ΔtseP cells, albeit to a lesser extent.
source: Western blot analysis not only confirmed the secretion of TseP and TsePN but also detected the secretion of TsePC, albeit to a lesser extent, in both wild-type and the ΔtseP cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: VgrG2 is the carrier protein for TseP delivery.
source: Considering that VgrG2 is the carrier protein for TseP delivery (Liang et al., 2021b), we next tested whether TsePN and TsePC could interact with VgrG2.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2021b.

claim: VgrG2 interacts directly with TsePN and TsePC.
source: Pull-down analysis showed direct interaction of VgrG2 with TsePN and TsePC, in contrast to the sfGFP and MBP negative controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TseP-mediated PG-hydrolysis produces NAM-NAG disaccharides and Tri/Tetra peptides.
source: When analyzing TseP-mediated PG-hydrolysis products using ultraperformance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS), we detected two distinctive peaks and determined their corresponding products to be NAM-NAG disaccharides and Tri/Tetra peptides (Figure 2A and B), the latter suggesting an amidase activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The released peptides were detected in samples treated with TsePN and the catalytically inactive C-terminal lysozyme mutant TsePE663A, but not with TsePC or its inactive TsePC-E663A mutant.
source: The released peptides were also detected in samples treated with TsePN and the catalytically inactive C-terminal lysozyme mutant TsePE663A (Liang et al., 2021b), but not with TsePC or its inactive TsePC-E663A mutant, indicating that the amidase activity is attributed to TsePN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and by citation to Liang et al., 2021b.

claim: The amidase activity is attributed to TsePN.
source: The released peptides were also detected in samples treated with TsePN and the catalytically inactive C-terminal lysozyme mutant TsePE663A (Liang et al., 2021b), but not with TsePC or its inactive TsePC-E663A mutant, indicating that the amidase activity is attributed to TsePN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TsePN contains a predicted Zn2+-binding domain with conserved residues H19, H23, H109, H339, H359, and E539.
source: Sequence comparison with known amidases suggests that the TsePN contains a predicted Zn2+-binding domain with several conserved residues H19, H23, H109, H339, H359, and E539 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and structural analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TsePN mutants with alanine substitutions at H19, H23, H109, H339, H359, and E539 showed significantly reduced amidase activity compared to TsePN.
source: Subsequent PG-digestion assays, coupled with UPLC-MS analysis, showed significantly reduced amidase activity in these mutants compared to TsePN (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EDTA abolished the amidase activity of TseP.
source: To test the role of metal ions for TseP's amidase activity, we added the chelating agent EDTA to the PG-digestion mixture, which abolished the amidase activity (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Adding Zn2+, but not Ca2+, restored the amidase function of TseP purified in the presence of EDTA.
source: PG-digestion assays revealed that adding Zn2+, but not Ca2+, restored the amidase function (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: TsiP can effectively inhibit both amidase activity and PG-hydrolysis activity of TseP, TsePN, and TsePC.
source: Enzymatic assays using purified PG showed that TsiP could effectively inhibit both amidase activity and PG-hydrolysis activity of TseP, TsePN, and TsePC (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TsiP interacts with both TsePC and TsePN.
source: Additionally, pull-down assays showed that TsiP interacts with not only TsePC but also TsePN (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Expression of TsePH339A restored Hcp secretion similar to wild-type TseP.
source: Secretion analysis revealed that expression of TsePH339A, but not the other mutants, restored Hcp secretion similar to wild-type TseP (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TsePH339A strain showed dynamic assembly of T6SS similar to the strain expressing the wild-type protein.
source: Observations of TssB-sfGFP sheath assembly in the Δ3eff TssB-sfGFP mutant further supported these findings, with the TsePH339A strain showing dynamic assembly of T6SS similar to the strain expressing the wild-type protein (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: The expression of TsePH339A and TseP showed comparable killing abilities in bacterial competition assays.
source: The expression of TsePH339A and TseP showed comparable killing abilities while the expression of other mutants demonstrated severely impaired killing activities as the T6SS-defective Δ3eff (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The amidase activity is not required for T6SS assembly.
source: Although it is unclear why the other mutations failed to complement, the H339A amidase-inactive mutation exhibiting a similar complementary role to wild-type TseP suggests that the amidase activity is not required for T6SS assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing TsePH339A complementation.

claim: TseP exhibited higher glycoside hydrolase activities than TsePC alone.
source: Results showed that TseP exhibited higher glycoside hydrolase activities than the TsePC alone, but there was no difference between TseP and the TsePH339A mutant (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no difference in glycoside hydrolase activity between TseP and the TsePH339A mutant.
source: Results showed that TseP exhibited higher glycoside hydrolase activities than the TsePC alone, but there was no difference between TseP and the TsePH339A mutant (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Amidase and lysozyme activities can each operate as functional modules within the TseP protein.
source: This indicates that amidase and lysozyme activities can each operate as functional modules within the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing independent activities.

claim: TseP homologs are broadly distributed across Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Homolog searching analysis reveals a broad distribution of TseP homologs across Gram-negative bacteria (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by homolog search analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AHA_1849 from Aeromonas hydrophila exhibits dual amidase and lysozyme activities.
source: Subsequent PG-hydrolysis and UPLC-MS analysis confirmed that both AHA_1849 and PSPTO_5204 exhibit dual amidase and lysozyme activities, capable of cleaving both peptide and glycan chains (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: PSPTO_5204 from Pseudomonas syringae exhibits dual amidase and lysozyme activities.
source: Subsequent PG-hydrolysis and UPLC-MS analysis confirmed that both AHA_1849 and PSPTO_5204 exhibit dual amidase and lysozyme activities, capable of cleaving both peptide and glycan chains (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The GC-content of TsePN is about 10% higher than that of TsePC.
source: Additionally, by analyzing the GC-contents of the two Aeromonas homologs, we found that the GC-content of TsePN is about 10% higher than that of TsePC and 10% lower than the upstream VgrG (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by GC content analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The GC-content of TsePN is 10% lower than the upstream VgrG.
source: Additionally, by analyzing the GC-contents of the two Aeromonas homologs, we found that the GC-content of TsePN is about 10% higher than that of TsePC and 10% lower than the upstream VgrG (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by GC content analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TsePN and TsePC domains may have been horizontally transferred and subsequently fused during evolution.
source: This suggests that these two domains might have been horizontally transferred and subsequently fused during evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GC content differences.

claim: TsePN-only homologs exist in various Aeromonas species, including a specific homolog in A. schubertii possessing only the TsePN domain.
source: We identified TsePN-only homologs in various Aeromonas species, including a specific homolog in A. schubertii possessing only the TsePN domain, whereas TsePC homologs were discovered in several other species, such as Fulvimonas soli and Vibrio campbellii (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by homolog search data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TsePC homologs were discovered in several species, such as Fulvimonas soli and Vibrio campbellii.
source: We identified TsePN-only homologs in various Aeromonas species, including a specific homolog in A. schubertii possessing only the TsePN domain, whereas TsePC homologs were discovered in several other species, such as Fulvimonas soli and Vibrio campbellii (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by homolog search data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TsePN and TsePC domains may have been fused through a recombination event, resulting in a chimeric, dual-functional TseP.
source: Considering the GC-content difference, we postulate that TsePN and TsePC domains may have been fused through a recombination event, resulting in a chimeric, dual-functional TseP.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the GC content analysis and homolog distribution.

claim: Both TseP and TsePC displayed more efficient digestion of purified PG from Gram-negative bacteria than the commonly used hen-egg lysozyme.
source: While testing TseP-mediated hydrolysis of purified PG from Gram-negative bacteria, we noticed that both TseP and TsePC displayed more efficient digestion than the commonly used hen-egg lysozyme (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The X-ray crystal structure of TsePC was determined to a resolution of 2.27 Å.
source: To further investigate this, we determined the X-ray crystal structure of TsePC to a resolution of 2.27 Å (Rwork = 0.189 and Rfree = 0.227) by molecular replacement with one molecule in the asymmetric unit (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Table 1.

claim: TsePC comprises a smaller lobe of seven helices and a larger lobe of ten helices, separated by a concave groove.
source: The crystal structure revealed that TsePC comprises a smaller lobe of seven helices and a larger lobe of ten helices, separated by a concave groove (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The surface electrostatic potential of TsePC consists of both electronegative and electropositive regions, unlike the predominantly electronegative groove of lysozyme.
source: The surface electrostatic potential of TsePC, calculated using the Adaptive Poisson-Boltzmann Solver (APBS), consists of both electronegative and electropositive regions, unlike the predominantly electronegative groove of lysozyme (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The electropositive surface of TsePC consists of residues R723 and K796.
source: The electropositive surface of TsePC consists of residues R723 and K796, with an adjacent residue Y720 corresponding to W62 in lysozyme, altering which is known to affect substrate binding (Maenaka et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5C and by citation to Maenaka et al., 1995.

claim: Y720 in TsePC corresponds to W62 in lysozyme, altering which is known to affect substrate binding.
source: The electropositive surface of TsePC consists of residues R723 and K796, with an adjacent residue Y720 corresponding to W62 in lysozyme, altering which is known to affect substrate binding (Maenaka et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maenaka et al., 1995.

claim: The previously predicted catalytic dyad (E655 and E663) was located near the groove in TsePC.
source: Additionally, the previously predicted catalytic dyad (E655 and E663) was located near the groove.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of TsePC.

claim: TsePC exhibits a less compact conformation with a notably wider groove compared to the typical lysozyme.
source: Although this structural arrangement resembles that of other lysozyme family members, TsePC exhibits a less compact conformation with a notably wider groove compared to the typical lysozyme (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The lysozyme possesses catalytic sites at E53 and D70 in the substrate-binding groove.
source: Previous studies have shown that the lysozyme possesses catalytic sites at E53 and D70 in the substrate-binding groove (Maenaka et al., 1995), while the active residues in the TsePC structure are E654 and E663, respectively (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maenaka et al., 1995.

claim: The active residues in the TsePC structure are E654 and E663.
source: Previous studies have shown that the lysozyme possesses catalytic sites at E53 and D70 in the substrate-binding groove (Maenaka et al., 1995), while the active residues in the TsePC structure are E654 and E663, respectively (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TsePC-E663D lost the activity, suggesting the greater distance within the groove requires this glutamate residue.
source: The results show that TsePC-E663D lost the activity, suggesting the greater distance within the groove requires this glutamate residue (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: TseP and TsePC failed to detect any PG-hydrolysis of B. subtilis PG, in contrast to the lysozyme.
source: To test whether TseP can degrade various cell walls, we purified PG from B. subtilis, a model Gram-positive bacterium, for use as substrate. However, we failed to detect any PG-hydrolysis treated with TseP or TsePC, in contrast to the lysozyme (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Purification of PG with NaOH treatment led to effective hydrolysis of PG by TseP and TsePC.
source: Further purification of PG with NaOH treatment, removing PG-associated peptides, led to effective hydrolysis of PG by TseP and TsePC, suggesting a difference in substrate accessibility between the lysozyme and TseP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a difference in substrate accessibility between the lysozyme and TseP.
source: Further purification of PG with NaOH treatment, removing PG-associated peptides, led to effective hydrolysis of PG by TseP and TsePC, suggesting a difference in substrate accessibility between the lysozyme and TseP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential hydrolysis.

claim: TsePC4+ retained E. coli PG-hydrolyzing activities.
source: Activity assays confirmed that TsePC4+ retained E. coli PG-hydrolyzing activities (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: B. subtilis cells were lysed effectively by TsePC4+ but not TsePC.
source: To test whether the engineered TsePC4+ was able to lyse B. subtilis, we treated B. subtilis cells with purified TsePC and TsePC4+ and found that cells were lysed effectively by TsePC4+ but not TsePC (Figure 6D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Modulating the surface charge is an effective strategy to expand the target range of PG-lysing effectors.
source: These results indicate that modulating the surface charge is an effective strategy to expand the target range of PG-lysing effectors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing TsePC4+ activity.

claim: TsePC4+ was secreted at a lower level than the wild-type TsePC.
source: Protein secretion analysis showed a significant TsePC4+ signal in secretion samples, despite at a lower level than the wild-type TsePC (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Survival of B. subtilis was significantly reduced when co-incubated with the ΔtseP mutant expressing the engineered TsePC4+ in a T6SS-dependent manner.
source: When B. subtilis was co-incubated with the ΔtseP mutant expressing the engineered TsePC4+ in liquid culture, survival of B. subtilis was significantly reduced in a T6SS-dependent manner (Figure 6F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The T6SS can be armed with engineered TsePC4+ to gain Gram-positive killing capabilities in a contact-independent manner.
source: These data collectively suggest that the T6SS can be armed with engineered TsePC4+ to gain Gram-positive killing capabilities in a contact-independent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing B. subtilis killing.

claim: TseP represents a novel family of dual-functional chimeric effectors, exhibiting both amidase and lysozyme activities.
source: Here, we report that TseP represents a novel family of dual-functional chimeric effectors, exhibiting both amidase and lysozyme activities (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminus of TseP serves a critical structural role in T6SS assembly.
source: Our study reveals that the N-terminus of TseP not only serves a critical structural role in T6SS assembly but also acts as a Zn2+-dependent amidase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The N-terminus of TseP acts as a Zn2+-dependent amidase.
source: Our study reveals that the N-terminus of TseP not only serves a critical structural role in T6SS assembly but also acts as a Zn2+-dependent amidase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The N- and C-domains of TseP are both secreted and functionally independent.
source: The N- and C-domains are both secreted and functionally independent, and may be subject to an evolutionary fusion event to form the chimeric full-length TseP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The N- and C-domains of TseP may be subject to an evolutionary fusion event to form the chimeric full-length TseP.
source: The N- and C-domains are both secreted and functionally independent, and may be subject to an evolutionary fusion event to form the chimeric full-length TseP.
evidence: This is a speculation based on GC content analysis and homolog distribution shown in Figure 4.

claim: Certain T6SSs are capable of translocating multiple PG-targeting effectors.
source: Among the known T6SS effectors, those targeting the bacterial PG layer represent a prevalent category. Certain T6SSs are capable of translocating multiple PG-targeting effectors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T6SS effectors.

claim: The H1-T6SS in Pseudomonas aeruginosa deploys Tse1 and Tse3.
source: For instance, the H1-T6SS in Pseudomonas aeruginosa deploys Tse1 and Tse3, while Vibrio cholerae secretes VgrG3 and TseH (Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020.

claim: Vibrio cholerae secretes VgrG3 and TseH.
source: For instance, the H1-T6SS in Pseudomonas aeruginosa deploys Tse1 and Tse3, while Vibrio cholerae secretes VgrG3 and TseH (Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020.

claim: Tse1 and TseH exhibit endopeptidase activities.
source: Tse1 and TseH exhibit endopeptidase activities, whereas Tse3 and VgrG3 have potent lysozyme activities (Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020.

claim: Tse3 and VgrG3 have potent lysozyme activities.
source: Tse1 and TseH exhibit endopeptidase activities, whereas Tse3 and VgrG3 have potent lysozyme activities (Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2011; Hood et al., 2010; Altindis et al., 2015; Hersch et al., 2020.

claim: It is relatively uncommon to identify effectors that possess dual functionality, capable of cleaving both the glycan chains and the cross-linked peptides within the bacterial cell wall.
source: Yet, it remains relatively uncommon to identify effectors that possess dual functionality, capable of cleaving both the glycan chains and the cross-linked peptides within the bacterial cell wall.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited examples of bifunctional effectors.

claim: Tse4 from A. baumannii is the sole established example of an effector that acts both as a transglycosylase to cleave the glycan strand and as an endopeptidase to cut the peptide cross-bridge.
source: To date, the sole established example is Tse4 from A. baumannii, which acts both as a transglycosylase to cleave the glycan strand and as an endopeptidase to cut the peptide cross-bridge (Le et al., 2021; Chou et al., 2012; Radkov et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Le et al., 2021; Chou et al., 2012; Radkov et al., 2022.

claim: TseP distinguishes itself from Tse4 with dual roles as a lysozyme and an amidase, as well as a structural role for T6SS assembly.
source: Our enzymatic assays reveal that TseP distinguishes itself from Tse4 with dual roles as a lysozyme and an amidase, as well as a structural role for T6SS assembly.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: TseP constitutes a new family of dual-functional effectors.
source: Further homology searches and biochemical validations of homolog activities substantiate that TseP constitutes a new family of dual-functional effectors.
evidence: This is supported by homolog analysis and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Effectors play a crucial structural role in T6SS assembly.
source: Our data demonstrate that the N-terminus of TseP can modulate T6SS assembly, which provides further evidence that effectors play a crucial structural role in T6SS assembly (Liang et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2021a; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2021a; Wu et al., 2020.

claim: The assembly of a non-contractile mutant T6SS in V. cholerae in the absence of effectors suggests that effectors might be needed to stabilize a polymerizing T6SS.
source: The assembly of a non-contractile mutant T6SS in V. cholerae in the absence of effectors suggests that effectors might be needed to stabilize a polymerizing T6SS (Stietz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stietz et al., 2020.

claim: Expressing TseP in the periplasm is highly toxic, but this toxicity is mitigated when catalytic mutations are introduced into the C-terminal lysozyme domain.
source: Previous studies have shown that expressing TseP in the periplasm is highly toxic, but this toxicity is mitigated when catalytic mutations are introduced into the C-terminal lysozyme domain (Liang et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2021b.

claim: The N-terminal amidase is either less toxic or is tightly regulated by the concentration of Zn2+ in the growth medium.
source: This indicates that the N-terminal amidase is either less toxic or is tightly regulated by the concentration of Zn2+ in the growth medium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of differential toxicity.

claim: The total intracellular Zn2+ concentration during growth in Lysogeny Broth (LB) has been reported to be around 0.1 mM.
source: Although the total intracellular Zn2+ concentration during growth in Lysogeny Broth (LB) has been reported to be around 0.1 mM—approximately 100 times higher than the Zn2+ level in the LB medium—the bioavailable (free) Zn2+ concentration within E. coli cells remains exceedingly low (Outten and O'Halloran, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Outten and O'Halloran, 2001.

claim: The bioavailable (free) Zn2+ concentration within E. coli cells remains exceedingly low.
source: Although the total intracellular Zn2+ concentration during growth in Lysogeny Broth (LB) has been reported to be around 0.1 mM—approximately 100 times higher than the Zn2+ level in the LB medium—the bioavailable (free) Zn2+ concentration within E. coli cells remains exceedingly low (Outten and O'Halloran, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Outten and O'Halloran, 2001.

claim: TseH activity is dependent on the environmental concentrations of Mg2+ and Ca2+.
source: A similar dependency on metal ions was observed with another cell-wall-targeting endopeptidase effector, TseH, whose activity is dependent on the environmental concentrations of Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Tang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2022.

claim: Metal ion dependencies might lead to misbelief about these effectors being cryptic or inactive, complicating the discovery and functional analysis of these important proteins.
source: Such metal ion dependencies might lead to misbelief about these effectors being cryptic or inactive, complicating the discovery and functional analysis of these important proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of metal ion dependencies.

claim: TseP is predicted to contain an EF-hand calcium-binding domain with a 'helix-loop-helix' motif.
source: TseP is predicted to contain an EF-hand calcium-binding domain with a 'helix-loop-helix' motif, a feature previously unreported in T6SS effectors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural prediction shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations introduced to the EF-hand domain did not reveal any critical effect on TseP functions under the conditions tested.
source: However, mutations introduced to this domain, aimed at exploring its role in T6SS assembly and TseP toxicity, did not reveal any critical effect on TseP functions under the conditions tested (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria generally prohibits the entry of cell-wall-lysing proteins.
source: Because the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria generally prohibits the entry of cell-wall-lysing proteins, the relatively exposed Gram-positive bacteria are likely more amenable to such treatments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell structure.

claim: The T6SS, exclusively found in Gram-negative bacteria, primarily targets Gram-negative species.
source: However, the T6SS, exclusively found in Gram-negative bacteria, primarily targets Gram-negative species.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T6SS distribution and function.

claim: Only two T6SSs, identified in Acidovorax citrulli and A. baumannii, have shown the capability to kill Gram-positive bacteria.
source: To date, only two T6SSs, identified in Acidovorax citrulli and A. baumannii (Le et al., 2021; Pei et al., 2022), have shown the capability to kill Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Le et al., 2021; Pei et al., 2022.

claim: No Gram-positive cell wall lysing effectors have been reported.
source: Additionally, no Gram-positive cell wall lysing effectors have been reported; for instance, Tse4 from A. baumannii cannot directly lyse B. subtilis cultures but requires T6SS delivery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of reported examples.

claim: Tse4 from A. baumannii cannot directly lyse B. subtilis cultures but requires T6SS delivery.
source: Additionally, no Gram-positive cell wall lysing effectors have been reported; for instance, Tse4 from A. baumannii cannot directly lyse B. subtilis cultures but requires T6SS delivery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tse4 function.

claim: The engineered TsePC represents the first effector variant capable of directly lysing B. subtilis cultures.
source: The engineered TsePC represents the first effector variant capable of directly lysing B. subtilis cultures, paying the way for engineering the diverse set of T6SS cell-wall-targeting effectors.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The insights from this research into T6SS and its diverse effectors signal promising directions for future work in microbial biology and antimicrobial therapy.
source: The insights from our research into T6SS and its diverse effectors signal promising directions for future work in microbial biology and antimicrobial therapy.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: When enhanced through protein engineering, T6SS effectors have the potential to address bacterial infections not only in medical settings but also in food safety and animal health.
source: When enhanced through protein engineering, these enzymes have the potential to address bacterial infections not only in medical settings but also in food safety and animal health.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications.
